subject: government

items.question: A student argues that American independence used 'old ideas, not new ones.' Which piece of evidence BEST supports this claim?
items.question_es: Un estudiante sostiene que la independencia usó 'ideas viejas, no nuevas'. ¿Qué evidencia apoya MEJOR esta afirmación?

options.A: The colonists invented the idea of natural rights in 1776.
options.B: Magna Carta (1215) already limited the king's power and protected life, liberty, and property.
options.C: The Constitution was written before the Declaration.
options.D: Greek democracy had no influence on American government.

distractor_rationale.A: Opposite of the claim; natural rights were inherited from Locke and earlier traditions.
distractor_rationale.B: Correct — Magna Carta predates 1776 by centuries and already limited royal power, showing the roots were old.
distractor_rationale.C: False chronology — the Declaration (1776) came before the Constitution (1787).
distractor_rationale.D: Incorrect — Greek democracy and the Roman republic were cited influences.

items.answer_explanation: The colonists drew on Magna Carta, Locke, and classical models — evidence the ideas were inherited and reshaped, not invented.

items.question: The Declaration lists natural rights and then a long list of grievances against King George III. Why place them together?
items.question_es: La Declaración enumera derechos naturales y luego agravios contra el rey. ¿Por qué juntarlos?

options.B: To describe how to run state governments
options.C: To request an apology from the king
options.D: To build an argument: rights + the king's violations justify separation

distractor_rationale.A: Length was not the purpose; the structure is an argument.
distractor_rationale.B: It does not outline state-government procedures.
distractor_rationale.C: The Declaration announces separation, not a request for apology.
distractor_rationale.D: Correct — universal rights (premise) + specific violations (evidence) → justified separation (conclusion).

items.answer_explanation: Grievances turn principle into justification — the logic of a government that may be altered when it violates rights.

items.question: The Great Compromise settled which major disagreement at the Constitutional Convention?
items.question_es: El Gran Compromiso resolvió ¿cuál desacuerdo importante en la Convención Constitucional?

options.A: Whether to keep the Articles of Confederation
options.B: Whether to have a president or a king
options.C: How states would be represented in Congress — by population or equally

distractor_rationale.A: That debate was settled by writing a new constitution, not by the Great Compromise.
distractor_rationale.B: The Convention rejected monarchy from the start.
distractor_rationale.C: Correct — a population-based House plus an equal-representation Senate reconciled large and small states.
distractor_rationale.D: Parties are not addressed by the compromise.

items.answer_explanation: The Virginia Plan (population) and New Jersey Plan (equal) were merged into a bicameral Congress.

items.question: Madison wrote that 'ambition must be made to counteract ambition.' Which design does this describe?
items.question_es: Madison escribió que 'la ambición debe contrarrestar la ambición'. ¿Qué diseño describe esto?

options.B: Checks and balances that let each branch limit the others

distractor_rationale.A: Popular sovereignty concerns the source of power, not inter-branch checks.
distractor_rationale.B: Correct — branches are set against each other so each checks the others' ambition.
distractor_rationale.C: Federalism divides nation/state power, a different limit.
distractor_rationale.D: Article V is unrelated to Madison's point here.

items.answer_explanation: Federalist No. 51's logic is structural: pit power against power through checks and balances.

remediation.next_step: Re-anchor on the primary source, re-teach the 3 vocabulary terms (EN/ES), then re-attempt a parallel item.

items.question: The First Amendment begins 'Congress shall make no law…'. Why phrase protections as limits on government?
items.question_es: La Primera Enmienda comienza 'El Congreso no hará ley…'. ¿Por qué expresar protecciones como límites al gobierno?

options.A: Because rights pre-exist government; the Constitution's job is to stop government from violating them
options.B: To show the government created these rights and may remove them
options.C: To give Congress more power over speech

distractor_rationale.A: Correct — natural-rights thinking: rights belong to people already; limits restrain government.
distractor_rationale.B: The framing implies the opposite — rights are not government gifts.
distractor_rationale.C: The clause restricts Congress, it does not expand its power.
distractor_rationale.D: Rights belong to persons, not to Congress.

items.answer_explanation: Phrasing rights as prohibitions limits government power rather than granting rights it could revoke.
